This bill updates several laws to help authorities handle the challenges of widespread encryption.
It would create new oversight and review processes, including a legislative review within 18 months of the changes starting.
The bill would limit industry assistance measures to serious offences punishable by at least three years in prison.
The bill would enhance oversight arrangements and provide review mechanisms.
It would add reporting requirements on the use of certain powers.
It would define 'systemic weakness' and 'systemic vulnerability' for technical reporting.
It would require the Attorney-General and the Minister for Communications to jointly approve technical capability notices.
It would impose 12-month time limits on technical assistance and capability notices.
It would limit the application of industry assistance measures to serious offences.
Telecommunications providers, law enforcement agencies, intelligence agencies, oversight bodies, and the Attorney-General are affected.

The majority voted in favour of an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-12-06.173.1) introduced by Senator [Mathias Cormann](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/mathias_cormann), which means it succeeded. ### Motion text > *At the end of the motion, add:* > *"and the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security conduct a review of the operation of the amendments made by this bill and report on that review by 3 April 2019."*

The Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 was introduced to address the erosion of law enforcement and security agencies' investigative capacity due to encryption, creating new industry assistance powers (technical assistance and technical capability notices) without mandating backdoors, expanding computer access warrants, and increasing penalties for failing to assist device access—citing that encryption affected 9 in 10 ASIO priority cases and 200 AFP operations, and encrypted intercepts rose from 3% in June 2013 to over 55% by July 2017.

Labor supported the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 after negotiating amendments to define “systemic weakness,” strengthen oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and the Commonwealth Ombudsman, and require further review, in order to address risks to national security, US security cooperation, and Australian technology businesses.

The speaker argued that the bill creates a systemic weakness in encrypted communications, threatening privacy, the tech industry, and civil liberties. They opposed rushed passage of the bill and the 50 pages of last-minute amendments, citing past failures like metadata laws that saw 350,000 requests per year, and warned that Australia would become a place where tech developers would avoid working.

Argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 addressed serious terrorism, child abuse, security and privacy issues, but criticised the government's handling and contradictory explanations. Supported targeted assistance powers while opposing systemic weaknesses, back doors and weakened encryption, and backed stronger Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security safeguards.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 risks weakening encryption without adequate judicial oversight, warning that 350,000 metadata requests—including from local councils—demonstrate how security powers can be misused.

The speaker argued the government rushed and politicised the encryption bill, refused judicial oversight for technical assistance and capability notices, and failed to define 'systemic weakness'. Labor reached a compromise to pass the bill before Christmas but maintained concerns.

Opposed the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018, arguing it would build a known vulnerability into encryption software that could be exploited by wrongdoers, and criticised the excessive extension of state power through security reforms including mandatory metadata retention. Also defended the member for Eden-Monaro’s comments and described the member for Hume’s comment as deeply offensive.

The MP criticised the government for rushing the encryption bill without proper consultation, arguing Labor secured amendments to clarify systemic weakness, add oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and the Ombudsman, and require Attorney-General and communications minister approval for technical capability notices. Labor remains concerned about the lack of judicial oversight for interception-related notices and will monitor the legislation, with the committee inquiry continuing into 2019 and a separate review by the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor within 18 months.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 requires balancing national security with individual privacy, noting that the government rushed the bill through the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security despite bipartisan efforts and 300 amendments on 15 previous national security bills. The speaker criticized Prime Minister Morrison and the Minister for Home Affairs for politicizing the process and ignoring submissions from Australian tech companies, while Labor proposed substantive amendments to address concerns from industry and civil society.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 is urgently needed to help law enforcement and national security agencies access encrypted communications used by criminals and terrorists, citing that 95% of ASIO’s top counterterrorism targets use encryption and referencing recent fatal attacks in Melbourne. The bill introduces new computer access warrants and industry assistance frameworks, prohibits systemic backdoors, and includes safeguards against mass surveillance, with the speaker urging parliamentary support for the bill and agreed amendments.

The speaker criticised the government's handling of the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018, arguing that the process was rushed and interfered with despite a consensus report from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security. They noted the bill is 175 pages, amends 10 acts, and introduces new compulsory powers against innocent third parties, and that the government tabled 173 amendments (covering 50 pages) informally at 6:30 am on the day of debate, with no formal response to the committee's 17 recommendations.

The bill would make it easier to call out the Australian Defence Force to respond to domestic violence, including terrorism, in Australia.
It would remove the current requirement that states and territories cannot protect themselves, and would let ministers consider whether the ADF would improve the response.

The bill would also expand contingent call-out to cover land and sea threats, not just aviation threats, and would add the Minister for Home Affairs as an alternative authorising minister for expedited call-out.
States and territories would no longer need to show they cannot protect themselves before requesting ADF support.
The ADF could be pre-authorised to respond to threats on land and at sea, as well as in the air.
The ADF would have to consult more with state and territory police.
Search, seizure and movement control powers would be simplified, expanded and clarified.
The distinction between general security areas and designated areas would be removed.
Acting ministers would be treated as substantive ministers for expedited call-out.
The Australian Defence Force, state and territory governments, the Minister for Home Affairs, and state and territory police.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-11-27.45.1) to pass the bill in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). Since the bill was already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does this bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1819a/19bd043), the main purpose of the bill is: > *to clarify and streamline the processes under which the Australian Defence Force (ADF) may be called out to protect Commonwealth interests and states and self-governing territories from domestic violence.* It was introduced following "*a Defence review of the ADF’s support to domestic counter-terrorism arrangements undertaken after the Lindt café siege in Sydney.*"

The Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018 was introduced to streamline legal procedures for deploying the ADF to support state and territory police in domestic security incidents, particularly terrorism. Key changes include lowering the threshold for call-outs, expanding contingent call-outs to state and territory interests, enabling multijurisdictional operations, simplifying ADF powers, and adding the Minister for Home Affairs as a named alternative minister for expedited call-outs.

The speaker announced Labor's support for the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, which makes it easier for states and territories to request ADF support, simplifies and expands ADF powers, enables pre-authorisation for land, sea and air threats, and enhances multi-jurisdictional responses. The government also tabled an amended explanatory memorandum providing clearer definitions of "specified circumstances" and "Commonwealth interests" as recommended by the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing it would make it easier for states and territories to request ADF support during terrorist attacks by removing complex criteria and enabling faster, multi-jurisdictional responses. The bill implements recommendations from a 2017 review prompted by the Lindt Cafe siege, adds the Minister for Home Affairs as an alternative minister for expedited call-outs, and extends contingent call-out to protect state and territory interests.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing it updates the legal framework for deploying the ADF domestically against terrorism, citing the 1978 Hilton bombing, the 1995 Aum Shinrikyo attack, and the 2014 Lindt Cafe siege as examples of evolving threats. He noted the bill expands ADF powers to search, detain persons, and operate across multiple jurisdictions, while maintaining civilian primacy and democratic oversight.

The speaker argued that the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018 should be passed to expedite ADF call-outs for terror threats, including by expanding authorising ministers to the Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Minister for Home Affairs, and Treasurer, and extending contingent call-outs to land and maritime threats, while clarifying that the ADF will not be used to disperse peaceful protests.

The Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018 lowers the threshold for state and territory requests for ADF assistance, introduces contingent call-outs for major events like the G20 and Commonwealth Games, and clarifies definitions including "domestic violence" to exclude peaceful protests. The bill was supported by Labor as a reasonable improvement following the Lindt cafe siege coroner's report.

The speaker argued for the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, which would lower the threshold for military call-out to allow the ADF to more easily support state and territory police during domestic terrorist incidents, citing the 2017 Etihad Airways bomb plot and the Lindt Cafe siege as examples of evolving threats. The bill was defended as a necessary update to legislation unchanged since 2000, with 27,000 calls to the National Security Hotline in the past year underscoring the ongoing threat level.

Labor supports the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, which simplifies call-out powers, allows pre-authorisation for events like the G20 or Commonwealth Games, and makes it easier for states to request ADF support while keeping state police as first responders. The bill was reviewed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights and the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee, leading to an amended explanatory memorandum clarifying definitions of specified circumstances, Commonwealth interest, and domestic violence.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing it would implement review recommendations, give ministers flexibility, and unlock ADF counterterrorism capabilities including the Tactical Assault Groups from the 2nd Commando Regiment and SASR. The bill removes the threshold requirement that states must be unable to protect themselves before requesting ADF support, and the speaker considered the Lindt Cafe siege had met the threshold for ADF involvement.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing it would streamline state and territory requests for ADF assistance in counterterrorism and other incidents, expand pre-authorisation for ADF response to land, sea and air threats, and enhance training cooperation with local authorities, while keeping police and emergency services as first responders.

Labor supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, which streamlines ADF call-out procedures for domestic counterterrorism by easing state/territory requests, expanding search and detention powers, enabling multijurisdictional response, and allowing pre-authorisation for threats on land, sea and air, while maintaining civilian control and state police as first responders.

Labor supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing that national security arrangements must remain agile against evolving terrorist threats. The speaker also commended the 5,622 ADF personnel involved in Operation Gold during the 2000 Sydney Olympics, including Joint Task Forces 112 and 643 under Brigadier Phil McNamara.

Supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, noting it has bipartisan support and that major events require safety coordination. Highlighted Bendigo and central Victoria as proud defence communities with a long history of hosting defence families.

Labor supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018 to simplify state requests for ADF support and expand its powers. The speaker also urged the government to broaden Australia’s critical infrastructure sectors beyond the current eight—noting the UK lists 13, the US 16, Canada 10 and Singapore 11—and to include electoral systems, citing 84 terrorism-related charges in four years and 734 cyber incidents affecting critical infrastructure in 2016–17.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing it streamlines ADF call-out procedures to assist state and territory police as secondary responders in terrorist incidents, while emphasising police remain primary first responders. The speaker also acknowledged the member for Canberra's warnings about cybersecurity threats to critical infrastructure and democratic processes.

The speaker argued that the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018 should not pass in its current form because it allows military call-out in undefined "specified circumstances" rather than only exceptional circumstances like terrorism, removes rights such as the right to silence, and grants broad legal immunity to defence personnel, contrary to warnings from the Law Council of Australia.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, endorsing the member for Canberra's proposal to include electoral systems as critical infrastructure, and criticised the Greens party for opposing anti-terrorism legislation, specifically citing their leader Senator Di Natale's view that foreign fighters should be allowed to return to Australia.

The Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018 was argued to modernise call-out powers for responding to complex terrorist threats, removing the requirement that states must be unable to protect themselves before the ADF can assist, and allowing pre-authorisation and expanded search, seizure and movement control powers.

According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd021): > *The purpose of the Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 (the Bill) is to amend the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) (the Act) to introduce a sponsorship framework for the sponsored family visa program. The proposed changes will:* > * *separate sponsorship assessment from the visa application process* > * *require the approval of persons as family sponsors before any relevant visa applications are made* > * *impose statutory obligations on persons who are or were approved as family sponsors and provide for enforceable sanctions if such obligations are not satisfied* > * *allow the Minister to refuse a sponsorship application and cancel and/or bar a family sponsor where inappropriate use of the program or serious offences are detected, especially those involving violence and* > * *improve the sharing of personal information between parties to the application and the program more generally.*

The majority voted in favour of [government amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-11-27.212.2), which means they'll be included in the bill. This new visa arrangement will allow parents to visit their Australian children without imposing an additional burden on Australia's healthcare system. In order to implement this new sponsored visa, there needs to be an assessable sponsorship framework for family sponsored visas. The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 will amend the Migration Act 1958 to introduce this framework. When the bill was first introduced, the framework was intended to apply to the partner program first and the rest of the family program later. To ensure that the sponsorship framework covers the requirements for the new parent visa, as well as all family sponsored visas, the bill requires government amendments.* > *To ensure that the new parent visa does not place any additional burden on Australia's healthcare system, the Australian child will be a financial guarantor for their parents' health costs. The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 introduces an assessable sponsorship framework for family sponsored visas, requiring sponsors to be assessed and approved before a visa application can proceed, with character checks shared with applicants. The bill aims to protect vulnerable visa applicants from domestic violence by allowing refusal or cancellation of sponsorship for sponsors with violent histories, initially applying to partner visas.

Labor supported the Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016, which introduces an assessable sponsorship framework for family visas, allowing refusal or cancellation of sponsors with a history of family violence. The party urged the government to create a new temporary visa with work rights for people on temporary visas fleeing domestic violence.

The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 strengthens the Migration Act to reduce family violence, including requiring pre-approval of sponsors for family stream visa applications and allowing character check results to be shared with the sponsored person. The amendments support the second action plan of the National Plan to Reduce Violence against Women and their Children 2010-2022.

Labor opposed the amendments to the Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016, arguing they assign financial responsibility for health costs to sponsored family visa holders with no guarantee the debt recovery function would not extend beyond parent visas, and that the government broke its election promise by failing to protect children and migrant communities.

This bill is part of a package that would create a system for approving people who sponsor family visa applicants.
The system would give officials the power to check sponsors, set legal duties for them, and punish rule-breaking with fines or other penalties.
The source describes only the work visa sponsorship framework already in the Migration Act and does not give a start date, threshold, or list of changes for this bill.
The bill would require sponsors to be assessed and approved before they can sponsor someone.
The bill would impose legal duties on sponsors.
The bill would allow civil penalties and administrative sanctions if sponsors break their duties.
The bill would let information be shared between relevant parties.
Sponsors of family visa applicants would be affected.

The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 was introduced to extend the assessable sponsorship framework to family sponsored visas, replacing unenforceable undertakings with statutory obligations enforced by civil penalties and administrative sanctions. The framework requires sponsor approval before visa applications, enables refusal, cancellation or barring of sponsors for family violence, and improves information sharing.
